nodes.name: Field trace
nodes.statement: The field trace ${\rm Tr}: {\mathbb F}_q \to {\mathbb F}_p$ is \[ {\rm Tr}(z) \mathrel{\mathop:}= \sum_{i=0}^{s-1} z^{p^i}. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: def:field-trace

nodes.name: Base additive character
nodes.statement: The base additive character $\psi:{\mathbb F}_q\to{\mathbb C}$ is \[ \psi(z) \mathrel{\mathop:}= \omega_p^{{\rm Tr}(z)}. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: def:base-character

nodes.name: Additive characters
nodes.statement: For $\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n$, define the additive character $\chi_\alpha: {\mathbb F}_q^n\to{\mathbb C}$ by \[ \chi_\alpha(x) \mathrel{\mathop:}= \psi(\langle \alpha, x \rangle) = \omega_p^{{\rm Tr}(\langle \alpha, x \rangle)}, \] where $\langle \alpha, x \rangle=\sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i x_i\in{\mathbb F}_q$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: def:additive-character

nodes.name: Expectation
nodes.statement: For a function $h:{\mathbb F}_q^n\to{\mathbb C}$, define its uniform expectation by \[ {\mathbb E}_{x\in{\mathbb F}_q^n}[h(x)] \mathrel{\mathop:}= \frac{1}{q^n}\sum_{x\in{\mathbb F}_q^n} h(x). \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: def:expectation

nodes.name: Inner product
nodes.statement: For functions $h_1,h_2:{\mathbb F}_q^n\to{\mathbb C}$, define \[ \langle h_1, h_2 \rangle \mathrel{\mathop:}= {\mathbb E}_{x\in{\mathbb F}_q^n}\left[h_1(x)\overline{h_2(x)}\right]. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: def:function-inner-product

nodes.name: $L_2$ norm
nodes.statement: For a function $h:{\mathbb F}_q^n\to{\mathbb C}$, define its $L_2$ norm by \[ \|h\|_2 \mathrel{\mathop:}= \left({\mathbb E}_{x\in{\mathbb F}_q^n}\left[\left\lvert{h(x)}\right\rvert^2\right]\right)^{1/2} = \sqrt{\langle h, h \rangle}. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: def:function-l2-norm

nodes.name: Fourier coefficient
nodes.statement: For $h:{\mathbb F}_q^n\to{\mathbb C}$ and $\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n$, define \[ \widehat h(\alpha) \mathrel{\mathop:}= \langle h, \chi_\alpha \rangle = {\mathbb E}_{x\in{\mathbb F}_q^n}\left[h(x)\overline{\chi_\alpha(x)}\right]. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: def:fourier-coefficient

nodes.name: Characters are orthonormal
nodes.statement: For every $\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb F}_q^n$, \[ \langle \chi_\alpha, \chi_\beta \rangle = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \alpha=\beta,\\ 0 & \text{if } \alpha\ne\beta. \end{cases} \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: lem:character-orthonormal

nodes.statement:
First observe that for every $\alpha, eta\in{\mathbb F}_q^n$ and every $x\in{\mathbb F}_q^n$, \[ \chi_\alpha(x)\overline{\chi_ eta(x)} = \omega_p^{{m Tr}(\langle \alpha, x angle)} \omega_p^{-{m Tr}(\langle  eta, x angle)} = \omega_p^{{m Tr}(\langle \alpha- eta, x angle)} = \chi_{\alpha- eta}(x), \] where we used the ${\mathbb F}_p$-linearity of the trace map. If $\alpha= eta$, then $\alpha- eta=0$, so $\chi_{\alpha- eta}(x)=1$ for every $x\in{\mathbb F}_q^n$. Hence \[ {\mathbb E}_{x\in{\mathbb F}_q^n}\left[\chi_\alpha(x)\overline{\chi_ eta(x)}ight] = {\mathbb E}_{x\in{\mathbb F}_q^n}[1] = 1. \] Now suppose $\alpha
e eta$. Let $\gamma \mathrel{\mathop:}= \alpha- eta$. Then $\gamma
e 0$, so there exists an index $j$ such that $\gamma_j
e 0$. Fix all coordinates of $x$ except $x_j$. For the fixed remaining coordinates, the map \[ x_j\mapsto \langle \gamma, x angle \] has the form \[ x_j\mapsto \gamma_j x_j + c \] for some constant $c\in{\mathbb F}_q$. Since $\gamma_j
e 0$, multiplication by $\gamma_j$ is a bijection on ${\mathbb F}_q$, and therefore the affine map $x_j\mapsto \gamma_jx_j+c$ is also a bijection on ${\mathbb F}_q$. Thus, as $x_j$ ranges uniformly over ${\mathbb F}_q$, the value $\langle \gamma, x angle$ also ranges uniformly over ${\mathbb F}_q$. Averaging first over $x_j$ and then over the remaining coordinates gives \[ {\mathbb E}_{x\in{\mathbb F}_q^n}\left[\chi_\gamma(x)ight] = {\mathbb E}_{t\in{\mathbb F}_q}\left[\omega_p^{{m Tr}(t)}ight]. \] It remains to show that this last average is zero. The trace map ${m Tr}:{\mathbb F}_q	o{\mathbb F}_p$ is a nonzero ${\mathbb F}_p$-linear map, so every fiber of ${m Tr}$ has the same cardinality. Since $\left\lvert{{\mathbb F}_q}ightvert=q$ and $\left\lvert{{\mathbb F}_p}ightvert=p$, each fiber has cardinality $q/p$. Therefore  egin{align*} {\mathbb E}_{t\in{\mathbb F}_q}\left[\omega_p^{{m Tr}(t)}ight] &=  rac{1}{q}\sum_{t\in{\mathbb F}_q}\omega_p^{{m Tr}(t)} \ &=  rac{1}{q}\sum_{r\in{\mathbb F}_p} \sum_{\substack{t\in{\mathbb F}_q\ {m Tr}(t)=r}} \omega_p^r \ &=  rac{1}{q}\sum_{r\in{\mathbb F}_p} rac{q}{p}\omega_p^r \ &=  rac{1}{p}\sum_{r\in{\mathbb F}_p}\omega_p^r \ &=0, \end{align*} because the sum of all $p$-th roots of unity is zero. Hence, if $\alpha
e eta$, then \[ {\mathbb E}_{x\in{\mathbb F}_q^n}\left[\chi_\alpha(x)\overline{\chi_ eta(x)}ight] = 0. \] Combining the two cases proves the stated orthogonality relation. The equivalent formulation follows by taking $ eta=0$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Fourier inversion
nodes.statement: For every function $h:{\mathbb F}_q^n\to{\mathbb C}$ we have \[ h(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n}\widehat h(\alpha)\chi_\alpha(x) \quad\text{for every }x\in{\mathbb F}_q^n. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: lem:fourier-inversion

nodes.statement: By \cref{lem:character-orthonormal}, the additive characters \[ \{\chi_\alpha : \alpha \in \mathbb F_q^n\} \] are orthonormal with respect to the inner product \[ \langle h_1,h_2\rangle = \mathbb E_{x\in \mathbb F_q^n} \left[h_1(x)\overline{h_2(x)}\right]. \] Moreover, these characters span the vector space of all complex-valued functions on \(\mathbb F_q^n\). Indeed, there are exactly \(q^n\) characters, and the space of functions \(\mathbb F_q^n\to\mathbb C\) has dimension \(q^n\). Since the characters are nonzero and pairwise orthogonal, they are linearly independent. Hence they form an orthonormal basis. Therefore every function \(h:\mathbb F_q^n\to\mathbb C\) has a unique expansion in this basis: \[ h = \sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb F_q^n} c_\alpha \chi_\alpha \] for some coefficients \(c_\alpha\in\mathbb C\). Taking the inner product of both sides with \(\chi_\beta\), we obtain \[ \langle h,\chi_\beta\rangle = \sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb F_q^n} c_\alpha \langle \chi_\alpha,\chi_\beta\rangle . \] By orthonormality, all terms in the sum vanish except the term \(\alpha=\beta\), and \(\langle \chi_\beta,\chi_\beta\rangle=1\). Hence \[ \langle h,\chi_\beta\rangle = c_\beta . \] By definition of the Fourier coefficient, \[ \widehat h(\beta)=\langle h,\chi_\beta\rangle . \] Thus \(c_\beta=\widehat h(\beta)\) for every \(\beta\in\mathbb F_q^n\). Therefore \[ h = \sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb F_q^n} \widehat h(\alpha)\chi_\alpha . \] Evaluating this identity at \(x\in\mathbb F_q^n\) gives the Fourier inversion formula \[ h(x) = \sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb F_q^n} \widehat h(\alpha)\chi_\alpha(x). \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Plancherel identity
nodes.statement: For every pair of functions $f,g:{\mathbb F}_q^n\to{\mathbb C}$, \[ \sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n} \widehat f(\alpha)\overline{\widehat g(\alpha)} = \langle f, g \rangle. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: lem:fourier-plancherel

nodes.statement: By \cref{lem:fourier-inversion}, \[ f=\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n}\widehat f(\alpha)\chi_\alpha . \] Taking the inner product with \(g\) and using linearity in the first argument gives \[ \langle f, g \rangle = \sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n} \widehat f(\alpha)\langle \chi_\alpha, g \rangle. \] Since \[ \langle \chi_\alpha, g \rangle = \overline{\langle g, \chi_\alpha \rangle} = \overline{\widehat g(\alpha)}, \] we obtain \[ \langle f, g \rangle = \sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n} \widehat f(\alpha)\overline{\widehat g(\alpha)}. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Parseval identity
nodes.statement: For every function $h:{\mathbb F}_q^n\to{\mathbb C}$, \[ \sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n}\left\lvert{\widehat h(\alpha)}\right\rvert^2 = \|h\|_2^2. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: lem:parseval-identity

nodes.statement: Apply \cref{lem:fourier-plancherel} with \(f=g=h\): \[ \sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n} \widehat h(\alpha)\overline{\widehat h(\alpha)} = \langle h, h \rangle. \] The left-hand side is \[ \sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n}\left\lvert{\widehat h(\alpha)}\right\rvert^2, \] and by the definitions of the inner product and the $L_2$ norm, the right-hand side is \[ \langle h, h \rangle = {\mathbb E}_{x\in{\mathbb F}_q^n}\left[\left\lvert{h(x)}\right\rvert^2\right] = \|h\|_2^2. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Nonzero field elements
nodes.statement: Write \[ {\mathbb F}_q^\times \mathrel{\mathop:}= \{c\in{\mathbb F}_q : c\ne 0\}. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: def:nonzero-field-elements

nodes.name: Fourier expansion of a finite-field-valued function
nodes.statement: Let $f:{\mathbb F}_q^n\to{\mathbb F}_q$. For each $c\in{\mathbb F}_q^\times$, define the $c$-phase lift \[ {\varphi}_{c}(x) \mathrel{\mathop:}= \omega_p^{{\rm Tr}(c f(x))}. \] The Fourier expansion of $f$ is the set $\{\varphi_c\}_{c\in {\mathbb F}_q^\times}$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: def:fourier-expansion-field-valued

nodes.name: Character-sum indicator
nodes.statement: For every $u,v\in{\mathbb F}_q$, \[ \mathbbm{1}[u=v] = \frac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in{\mathbb F}_q}\omega_p^{{\rm Tr}(c(u-v))}. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: lem:character-sum-indicator

nodes.statement:
For each $z \in {\mathbb F}_q$ we define \[ \psi(z) \mathrel{\mathop:}= \omega_p^{{m Tr}(z)} \] be the standard additive character of \({\mathbb F}_q\). We prove that, for every \(t\in {\mathbb F}_q\), \[ \mathbbm{1}[t=0] =  rac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in{\mathbb F}_q}\psi(ct). \] The desired statement follows by taking \(t=u-v\). If \(t=0\), then \(ct=0\) for every \(c\in{\mathbb F}_q\), so \[  rac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in{\mathbb F}_q}\psi(ct) =  rac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in{\mathbb F}_q}1 = 1. \] Now suppose \(t
eq 0\). Then multiplication by \(t\) is a bijection \({\mathbb F}_q	o{\mathbb F}_q\), so \[ \sum_{c\in{\mathbb F}_q}\psi(ct) = \sum_{z\in{\mathbb F}_q}\psi(z). \] We claim that the latter sum is \(0\). Let \[ S \mathrel{\mathop:}= \sum_{z\in{\mathbb F}_q}\psi(z). \] Since \({m Tr}:{\mathbb F}_q	o{\mathbb F}_p\) is a nonzero \({\mathbb F}_p\)-linear map, it is surjective. Hence there exists \(a\in{\mathbb F}_q\) such that \({m Tr}(a)=1\). Using the bijection \(z\mapsto z+a\), we get \[ S = \sum_{z\in{\mathbb F}_q}\psi(z+a) = \sum_{z\in{\mathbb F}_q}\omega_p^{{m Tr}(z+a)} = \sum_{z\in{\mathbb F}_q}\omega_p^{{m Tr}(z)}\omega_p^{{m Tr}(a)} = \omega_p S. \] Since \(\omega_p
eq 1\), this implies \(S=0\). Therefore, when \(t
eq 0\), \[  rac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in{\mathbb F}_q}\psi(ct)=0. \] Combining the two cases gives \[ \mathbbm{1}[t=0] =  rac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in{\mathbb F}_q}\omega_p^{{m Tr}(ct)}. \] Substituting \(t=u-v\), we obtain \[ \mathbbm{1}[u=v] =  rac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in{\mathbb F}_q}\omega_p^{{m Tr}(c(u-v))}. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Relative Hamming distance
nodes.statement: For $f,g:{\mathbb F}_q^n\to{\mathbb F}_q$, define \[ \delta(f,g) \mathrel{\mathop:}= \Pr_{x\in{\mathbb F}_q^n}\left[f(x)\ne g(x)\right]. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: def:relative-hamming-distance

nodes.name: Linear functions
nodes.statement: For $\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n$, define the linear scalar function $\ell_\alpha:{\mathbb F}_q^n\to{\mathbb F}_q$ by \[ \ell_\alpha(x) \mathrel{\mathop:}= \langle \alpha, x \rangle. \] A function $h:{\mathbb F}_q^n\to{\mathbb F}_q$ is linear if $h=\ell_\alpha$ for some $\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n$. The finite set of all linear scalar functions is \[ \ensuremath{\mathcal{LIN}} \mathrel{\mathop:}= \left\{\ell_\alpha \mid \alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n\right\}. \]
nodes.label: def:linear-functions

nodes.name: Distance to linearity
nodes.statement: The distance from $f:{\mathbb F}_q^n\to{\mathbb F}_q$ to linearity is \[ \delta(f,\ensuremath{\mathcal{LIN}}) \mathrel{\mathop:}= \min_{g\in\ensuremath{\mathcal{LIN}}}\delta(f,g). \]
nodes.label: def:distance-to-linearity

nodes.name: Well-separatedness of $\lin$
nodes.statement: For any distinct $f,g \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{LIN}}$, one has $\delta(f,g)= 1-1/|{\mathbb F}|$.
nodes.label: lem:linear-set-well-separated

nodes.statement: Let $a,b \in {\mathbb F}^n$ be the unique vectors such that $f(x) = \langle a, x\rangle$ and $g(x) = \langle b, x\rangle$ for each $x$. Let $c = a-b$, which must be a non-zero vector. In particular, there exists $i \in [n]$ such that $c_i \neq 0$. Take any permutation $\sigma: [n] \rightarrow [n]$ such that $\sigma(i)=n$. Then \begin{align*} \delta(f,g) & = 1- \Pr_{x \sim {\mathbb F}^n}[\langle c, x\rangle =0] \\ & = 1 - \frac{1}{|{\mathbb F}|^{n-1}}\sum_{x_1,\dots,x_{n-1} \in {\mathbb F}}\frac{1}{|{\mathbb F}|}\sum_{x_n \in {\mathbb F}} \mathbbm{1}[c_i \cdot x_n = -\sum_{j \in [n]\setminus {i}} c_j \cdot x_{\sigma(j)}] \\ & = 1 - \frac{1}{|{\mathbb F}|^{n-1}}\sum_{x_1,\dots,x_{n-1} \in {\mathbb F}}\frac{1}{|{\mathbb F}|}\sum_{x_n \in {\mathbb F}} \mathbbm{1}[x_n = -c_i^{-1} \cdot \sum_{j \in [n]\setminus {i}} c_j \cdot x_{\sigma(j)}] \end{align*} where the last equality follows because $c_i \neq 0$. Now note that $\mathbbm{1}[x_n = -c_i^{-1} \cdot \sum_{j \in [n]\setminus {i}} c_j \cdot x_{\sigma(j)}]$ evaluates to $1$ for exactly one value of $x_n$. Thus we continue from above and get \begin{align*} \delta(f,g) = 1-\frac{1}{|{\mathbb F}|^{n-1}}\sum_{x_1,\dots,x_{n-1} \in {\mathbb F}}\frac{1}{|{\mathbb F}|} = 1-\frac{1}{|{\mathbb F}|} \, . \end{align*}

nodes.name: Distance formula
nodes.statement: Let $f,g:{\mathbb F}_q^n\to{\mathbb F}_q$. Let $\{{\varphi}_{c}\}_{c\in{\mathbb F}_q^\times}$ and $\{{\gamma}_{c}\}_{c\in{\mathbb F}_q^\times}$ be their Fourier expansions. Then \[ \delta(f,g) = 1-\frac{1}{q}\left(1+ \sum_{c\in{\mathbb F}_q^\times} \langle {\varphi}_{c}, {\gamma}_{c} \rangle \right). \]
nodes.label: lem:distance-formula

nodes.statement: By \cref{lem:character-sum-indicator}, \[ \Pr_x[f(x)=g(x)] = {\mathbb E}_x\left[\frac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in{\mathbb F}_q} \omega_p^{{\rm Tr}(c(f(x)-g(x)))}\right]. \] The term $c=0$ contributes $1/q$. For $c\ne 0$, \[ \omega_p^{{\rm Tr}(c(f(x)-g(x)))} = {\varphi}_{c}(x)\overline{{\gamma}_{c}(x)}. \] Therefore \[ \Pr_x[f(x)=g(x)] =\frac{1}{q}\left(1+\sum_{c\in{\mathbb F}_q^\times} \langle {\varphi}_{c}, {\gamma}_{c} \rangle \right), \] which gives the first formula after using $\delta(f,g)=1-\Pr_x[f(x)=g(x)]$.

nodes.name: Fourier expansion of a linear function
nodes.statement: Fix $\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n$ and let $\{\lambda_c\}_{c \in {\mathbb F}_q^\times}$ be the Fourier expansion of $\ell_\alpha$. Then \[ \lambda_{c}=\chi_{c\alpha}. \]
nodes.label: lem:linear-function-fourier-expansion

nodes.statement: For every $x\in{\mathbb F}_q^n$, \[ \lambda_{c}(x) = \omega_p^{{\rm Tr}(c\langle \alpha, x \rangle)} = \omega_p^{{\rm Tr}(\langle c\alpha, x \rangle)} = \chi_{c\alpha}(x). \]

nodes.name: Linear Fourier score
nodes.statement: For $f:{\mathbb F}_q^n\to{\mathbb F}_q$ and $\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n$, define the linear Fourier score of $f$ at $\alpha$ by \[ S_\alpha(f) \mathrel{\mathop:}= \sum_{c\in{\mathbb F}_q^\times} \widehat{{\varphi}_{c}}(c\alpha), \] where $\{{\varphi}_{c}\}_{c \in {\mathbb F}_q^\times}$ is the Fourier expansion of $f$.
nodes.label: def:linear-fourier-score

nodes.name: Distance to linearity in Fourier form
nodes.statement: Let $f:{\mathbb F}_q^n\to{\mathbb F}_q$ have Fourier expansion $\{{\varphi}_{c}\}_{c\in{\mathbb F}_q^\times}$. Then \[ \delta(f,\ensuremath{\mathcal{LIN}}) = 1-\frac{1}{q}\left(1+ \max_{\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n} S_\alpha(f) \right). \] Moreover, for every $\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n$, the score $S_\alpha(f)$ is real and satisfies $-1\le S_\alpha(f)\le q-1$.
nodes.label: lem:distance-to-linearity-fourier

nodes.statement: Apply \cref{lem:distance-formula} with $g=\ell_\alpha$ and use \cref{lem:linear-function-fourier-expansion}. This gives \[ \delta(f,\ell_\alpha) =1-\frac{1}{q}\left(1+ S_\alpha(f) \right). \] Taking the minimum over $\alpha$ gives the claimed formula for $\delta(f,\ensuremath{\mathcal{LIN}})$. For fixed $\alpha$, the same formula expresses $S_\alpha(f)$ as $q(1-\delta(f,\ell_\alpha))-1$. Hence $S_\alpha(f)$ is real, and since $0\le \delta(f,\ell_\alpha)\le 1$, we get $-1\le S_\alpha(f)\le q-1$.

nodes.name: Finite-field BLR test
nodes.statement: Given oracle access to $f:{\mathbb F}_q^n\to{\mathbb F}_q$, the finite-field BLR verifier $\ensuremath{\mathsf{V}_{\mathsf{BLR}}^f}$ samples $a,b\in{\mathbb F}_q^\times$ and $x,y\in{\mathbb F}_q^n$ independently and uniformly at random, and accepts iff \[ a f(x)+b f(y)=f(ax+by). \] That is, \[ \ensuremath{\mathsf{V}_{\mathsf{BLR}}^f}=1 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a f(x)+b f(y)=f(ax+by). \]
nodes.label: def:finite-field-blr-test

nodes.name: Completeness
nodes.statement: If $f\in\ensuremath{\mathcal{LIN}}$, then \[ \Pr[\ensuremath{\mathsf{V}_{\mathsf{BLR}}^f}=1]=1. \]
nodes.label: lem:blr-completeness

nodes.statement: If $f=\ell_\alpha$ for some $\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n$, then for every $a,b\in{\mathbb F}_q^\times$ and $x,y\in{\mathbb F}_q^n$, \[ f(ax+by) =\langle \alpha, ax+by \rangle =a\langle \alpha, x \rangle+b\langle \alpha, y \rangle =a f(x)+b f(y). \] Thus the verifier accepts for every choice of randomness.

nodes.name: Exact BLR acceptance formula
nodes.statement: Let $f:{\mathbb F}_q^n\to{\mathbb F}_q$. Then \[ \Pr[\ensuremath{\mathsf{V}_{\mathsf{BLR}}^f}=1] = \frac{1}{q}\left(1+\frac{1}{(q-1)^2} \sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n} S_\alpha(f)^3 \right). \]
nodes.label: lem:exact-blr-acceptance

nodes.statement: By \cref{lem:character-sum-indicator}, for fixed $a,b,x,y$, \[ \mathbbm{1}[a f(x)+b f(y)=f(ax+by)] =\frac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in{\mathbb F}_q} \omega_p^{{\rm Tr}(c(a f(x)+b f(y)-f(ax+by)))}. \] Taking expectation gives \[ \Pr[\ensuremath{\mathsf{V}_{\mathsf{BLR}}^f}=1] =\frac{1}{q}+\frac{1}{q}{\mathbb E}_{a,b,x,y} \left[\sum_{c\in{\mathbb F}_q^\times} {\varphi}_{ca}(x){\varphi}_{cb}(y) {\varphi}_{-c}(ax+by) \right]. \] Expand the three complex-valued functions into their Fourier expansions: \begin{align*} &{\mathbb E}_{a,b,x,y} \left[\sum_{c\in{\mathbb F}_q^\times} {\varphi}_{ca}(x){\varphi}_{cb}(y) {\varphi}_{-c}(ax+by) \right] \\ &={\mathbb E}_{a,b}\left[\sum_{c\in{\mathbb F}_q^\times} \sum_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in{\mathbb F}_q^n} \widehat{{\varphi}_{ca}}(\alpha) \widehat{{\varphi}_{cb}}(\beta) \widehat{{\varphi}_{-c}}(\gamma) {\mathbb E}_{x,y}\left[ \chi_\alpha(x)\chi_\beta(y)\chi_\gamma(ax+by) \right] \right]. \end{align*} Since \[ \chi_\gamma(ax+by)=\chi_{a\gamma}(x)\chi_{b\gamma}(y), \] \cref{lem:character-orthonormal} implies that the inner expectation is $1$ exactly when \[ \alpha+a\gamma=0 \quad\text{and}\quad \beta+b\gamma=0, \] and is $0$ otherwise. Therefore the last display equals \[ {\mathbb E}_{a,b}\left[\sum_{c\in{\mathbb F}_q^\times} \sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n} \widehat{{\varphi}_{ca}}(\alpha) \widehat{{\varphi}_{cb}}(a^{-1}b\alpha) \widehat{{\varphi}_{-c}}(-a^{-1}\alpha) \right]. \] Substitute $\alpha=ca\eta$. Then this becomes \[ {\mathbb E}_{a,b}\left[\sum_{c\in{\mathbb F}_q^\times} \sum_{\eta\in{\mathbb F}_q^n} \widehat{{\varphi}_{ca}}(ca\eta) \widehat{{\varphi}_{cb}}(cb\eta) \widehat{{\varphi}_{-c}}(-c\eta) \right]. \] As $a,b,c$ range over ${\mathbb F}_q^\times$, so do $ca$, $cb$, and $-c$. Hence this equals \[ \frac{1}{(q-1)^2} \sum_{\eta\in{\mathbb F}_q^n} \left(\sum_{d\in{\mathbb F}_q^\times} \widehat{{\varphi}_{d}}(d\eta) \right)^3 =\frac{1}{(q-1)^2}\sum_{\eta\in{\mathbb F}_q^n}S_\eta(f)^3. \] Substituting into the expression for $\Pr[\ensuremath{\mathsf{V}_{\mathsf{BLR}}^f}=1]$ proves the claim.

nodes.name: Second moment bound
nodes.statement: For every $f:{\mathbb F}_q^n\to{\mathbb F}_q$, one has \[ \sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n} S_\alpha(f)^2 \le (q-1)^2. \]
nodes.label: lem:second-moment-bound

nodes.statement: Expanding the square gives \[ \sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n} S_\alpha(f)^2 =\sum_{a,b\in{\mathbb F}_q^\times} \sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n} \widehat{{\varphi}_{a}}(a\alpha) \widehat{{\varphi}_{b}}(b\alpha). \] For fixed $a,b\in{\mathbb F}_q^\times$, Cauchy-Schwarz and \cref{lem:parseval-identity} give \begin{align*} \left\lvert{\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n} \widehat{{\varphi}_{a}}(a\alpha) \widehat{{\varphi}_{b}}(b\alpha)}\right\rvert &\le \left(\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n}\left\lvert{\widehat{{\varphi}_{a}}(a\alpha)}\right\rvert^2\right)^{1/2} \left(\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n}\left\lvert{\widehat{{\varphi}_{b}}(b\alpha)}\right\rvert^2\right)^{1/2} \\ &=1. \end{align*} The equality uses that multiplication by $a$ and by $b$ permutes ${\mathbb F}_q^n$, and that Parseval plus $\left\lvert{{\varphi}_{a}(x)}\right\rvert=\left\lvert{{\varphi}_{b}(x)}\right\rvert=1$ for every $x$ make both squared $L_2$ norms equal to \(1\). Summing over the $(q-1)^2$ choices of $(a,b)$ gives the result.

nodes.name: Soundness of the finite-field BLR test
nodes.statement: For every function $f:{\mathbb F}_q^n\to{\mathbb F}_q$, one has \[ \Pr[\ensuremath{\mathsf{V}_{\mathsf{BLR}}^f}=1] \le 1-\delta(f,\ensuremath{\mathcal{LIN}}). \]
nodes.label: thm:finite-field-blr-soundness

nodes.statement: Let $S_\alpha(f)$ be as in \cref{def:linear-fourier-score}, and let \[ M \mathrel{\mathop:}= \max_{\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n}S_\alpha(f). \] By \cref{lem:distance-to-linearity-fourier}, \[ 1-\delta(f,\ensuremath{\mathcal{LIN}})=\frac{1}{q}(1+M). \] By \cref{lem:distance-to-linearity-fourier}, each $S_\alpha(f)$ is real and $S_\alpha(f)\le M$. Therefore $S_\alpha(f)^3\le M S_\alpha(f)^2$ for every $\alpha$, because $S_\alpha(f)^2\ge 0$. Using \cref{lem:exact-blr-acceptance} and \cref{lem:second-moment-bound}, \begin{align*} \Pr[\ensuremath{\mathsf{V}_{\mathsf{BLR}}^f}=1] &=\frac{1}{q}\left(1+\frac{1}{(q-1)^2} \sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n}S_\alpha(f)^3\right) \\ &\le \frac{1}{q}\left(1+\frac{M}{(q-1)^2} \sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb F}_q^n}S_\alpha(f)^2\right) \\ &\le \frac{1}{q}(1+M) \\ &=1-\delta(f,\ensuremath{\mathcal{LIN}}). \end{align*}

nodes.name: $\sigma$ inner product.
nodes.statement: The $\sigma$ inner product between matrices $A$ and $B$ is defined as \begin{equation} \langle A, B \rangle_{\sigma} = {\rm Tr}(A^* B \sigma), \end{equation} where $\sigma \geq 0$ and $A^*$ denotes conjugate-transpose.
nodes.label: sigmaInner

nodes.name: $(\epsilon, \sigma)$-representation.
nodes.statement: Given a finite group \(G\), an integer \(d \geq 1, \varepsilon \geq 0\), and a \(d\)-dimensional positive semidefinite matrix \(\sigma\) with trace 1 , an \((\varepsilon, \sigma)\)-representation of \(G\) is a map \(f: G \rightarrow U_{d}(\mathbb{C})\), to the \(d \times d\) unitary matrices, such that \begin{equation} \mathbb{E}_{x, y \in G} \Re\left(\left\langle f(x)^{*} f(y), f\left(x^{-1} y\right)\right\rangle_{\sigma}\right) \geq 1-\varepsilon, \end{equation} where $\Re$ denotes taking real part of the inner product.
nodes.label: approx-representation

nodes.name: $\sigma$-norm Square
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma$ be positive semidefinite and let $A, B$ be matrices of the same dimension. Then \[ \|A - B\|_\sigma^2 = \|A\|_\sigma^2 + \|B\|_\sigma^2 - 2\,\Re\langle A, B \rangle_\sigma. \]
nodes.label: sigmaNormSqSub

nodes.statement: Expanding by linearity of the inner product, \[ \|A-B\|_\sigma^2 = \Re\langle A-B, A-B \rangle_\sigma = \|A\|_\sigma^2 + \|B\|_\sigma^2 - \Re\langle A, B \rangle_\sigma - \Re\langle B, A \rangle_\sigma. \] Since $\sigma$ is Hermitian, $\langle B, A \rangle_\sigma = \overline{\langle A, B \rangle_\sigma}$, so the two cross terms have the same real part, yielding $-2\,\Re\langle A, B \rangle_\sigma$.

nodes.name: Regular representation
nodes.statement: Let $R: G \rightarrow \mathbb{C}[G]$ be a regular representation where $\{\mbox{$ | g \rangle $}, g\in G\}$ forms a basis of \(\mathbb{C}[G]\). The representation is given by \begin{equation} R(x) \mbox{$ | g \rangle $} = \mbox{$ | xg \rangle $}. \end{equation}
nodes.label: RegularRep

nodes.name: Maschke's theorem
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite group and let $\rho : G \to \mathrm{GL}(V)$ be a finite-dimensional representation over $\mathbb{C}$. Then $\rho$ is completely reducible. In particular, there exists a decomposition \begin{equation} \rho \cong \bigoplus_{m} r_m \, \rho_m, \end{equation} where $\{\rho_m\}$ is a set of inequivalent irreducible representations of $G$, and $r_m \in \mathbb{Z}^+$ are the multiplicities.
nodes.label: Maschke

nodes.name: Decomposition of the regular representation
nodes.statement: Let $R : G \to \mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{C}[G])$ be the regular representation of a finite group $G$. Then \begin{equation} R \cong \bigoplus_{\rho \in \widehat{G}} d_\rho \, \rho, \end{equation} where $\widehat{G}$ is a complete set of inequivalent irreducible representations of $G$, and $d_\rho = \dim(V_\rho)$ is the dimension of $\rho$.
nodes.label: RegDecompIrrep

nodes.name: Character of regular representation.
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite group and $\sum_\rho$ denotes summing over the complete set of inequivalent irreps $\hat{G}$ \begin{equation} \sum_{\rho \in \hat{G}} d_{\rho} \operatorname{Tr}(\rho(x))=|G| \delta_{x, e}. \end{equation}
nodes.label: regular_repr_character

nodes.name: Group fourier transform
nodes.statement: Let $f: G \rightarrow U_d(\mathbb{C})$ be a map and \(\rho: G \rightarrow U_{d_{\rho}}(\mathbb{C})\) be a unitary irrep. The fourier transform of $f$ at the representation $\rho$ is denoted by $\hat{f}$: \begin{equation} \hat{f}(\rho)=\mathbb{E}_{x \in G} f(x) \otimes \overline{\rho(x)}, \end{equation} where $\overline{\rho(x)}$ denotes complex conjugate of $\rho(x)$.
nodes.label: GroupFourier

nodes.name: Gowers-Hatami
nodes.statement: Let \(G\) be a finite group, \(\varepsilon \geq 0\), and \(f: G \rightarrow U_{d}(\mathbb{C})\) an \((\varepsilon, \sigma)\)-representation of \(G\). Then there exists a \(d^{\prime} \geq d\), an isometry \(V: \mathbb{C}^{d} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}^{d^{\prime}}\), and a representation \(g: G \rightarrow U_{d^{\prime}}(\mathbb{C})\) such that \begin{equation} \mathbb{E}_{x \in G}\left\|f(x)-V^{*} g(x) V\right\|_{\sigma}^{2} \leq 2 \varepsilon. \end{equation}
nodes.label: gowers-hatami

nodes.name: Gowers-Hatami Pair-Correlation
nodes.statement: Let \(G\) be a finite group, \(\varepsilon \geq 0\), and \(\rho: G \rightarrow U(\mathcal{H})\) an \((\varepsilon, \sigma)\)-representation of \(G\) on space $\mathcal{H}$. Define the pair-correlation of $\rho$ as: \begin{equation} \mathcal{C}(\rho) := \mathbb{E}_{x,y \in G} \Re \langle \rho(y)\rho(x), \rho(yx) \rangle_\sigma. \end{equation} Then there exists an isometry \(V: \mathcal{H} \rightarrow \mathcal{H}^\prime\) to a different space $\mathcal{H}^\prime$, and an exact representation \(\rho^\prime: G \rightarrow U(\mathcal{H}^\prime)\) such that the average correlation between $\rho$ and $\rho^\prime$ is exactly the pair-correlation, which is bounded by $1-\varepsilon$: \begin{equation} \mathbb{E}_{x \in G} \Re \langle \rho(x), V^{*} \rho^\prime(x) V\rangle_{\sigma} = \mathcal{C}(\rho) \geq 1-\varepsilon. \end{equation}
nodes.label: gowers-hatami-correlation

nodes.statement:
Here $\mathcal{H}^\prime = L(G, \mathcal{H})$ is the space of functions $f: G 	o \mathcal{H}$. Let the isometry be defined by the action of the approximate representation on a state $u\in \mathcal{H}$ as  egin{eqnarray} &V:& \mathcal{H} 	o L(G, \mathcal{H}), \ & V(u):& G 	o \mathcal{H}, \quad x \mapsto ho(x)(u), \quad  orall x \in G. \end{eqnarray} The adjoint map $V^*$ is defined as the unique map such that for all $u \in \mathcal{H}$ and $f \in L(G, \mathcal{H})$,  egin{equation} \langle V(u), f angle_{L(G, \mathcal{H})} = \langle u, V^*(f) angle_{\mathcal{H}}. \end{equation} In particular, $V^*$ is explicitly given by the group average:  egin{eqnarray} &V^*:& L(G, \mathcal{H}) 	o \mathcal{H}, \ &V^*(f)& = \mathbb{E}_{x \in G} \left[ ho^*(x) f(x) ight]. \end{eqnarray} The exact representation is given by the right regular representation on $L(G, \mathcal{H})$:  egin{eqnarray} &ho^\prime:& G 	o U(L(G, \mathcal{H})), \ &(ho^\prime(x)f)(y)& = f(yx), \quad  orall x,y \in G. \end{eqnarray} $V$ is an isometry because $ho(x)$ is unitary, yielding:  egin{equation} V^* V(u) = \mathbb{E}_{x \in G} \left[ ho^*(x) ho(x)(u) ight] = \mathbb{E}_{x \in G} [u] = u. \end{equation} The compression of the exact representation ``averages'' over group multiplication. nodes.name: Gowers-Hatami-2
nodes.statement: Let \(G\) be a finite group, \(\varepsilon \geq 0\), and \(\rho: G \rightarrow U(\mathcal{H})\) an \((\varepsilon, \sigma)\)-representation of \(G\) on space $\mathcal{H}=\mathbb{C}^{d}$. Then there exists an isometry \(V: \mathcal{H} \rightarrow \mathcal{H}^\prime\) to a different space $\mathcal{H}^\prime$, and a representation \(\rho^\prime: G \rightarrow \mathcal{H}^\prime\) such that \begin{equation} \mathbb{E}_{x \in G}\left\|\rho(x)-V^{*} \rho^\prime(x) V\right\|_{\sigma}^{2} \leq 2 \varepsilon. \end{equation}
nodes.label: gowers-hatami-2

nodes.statement: A regular-representation proof of the Gowers-Hatami theorem appears in Morel's slides~\cite{Morel20}, following the original Gowers-Hatami theorem~\cite{GowHat17}. The rest of the proof follows by expanding the $\sigma$-norm, bounding the norm of $\mathbb{E}_{x \in G} V^* \rho^\prime(x) V$ and applying the definition of $(\varepsilon, \sigma)$-representation. In particular, we have \begin{eqnarray} & &\mathbb{E}_{x \in G}\left\|\rho(x)-V^{*} \rho^\prime(x) V\right\|_{\sigma}^{2} \\ &= & \mathbb{E}_{x \in G} \| \rho(x) \|_\sigma^2 + \mathbb{E}_{x \in G} \|V^* \rho^\prime(x) V\|_\sigma^2 - 2 \mathbb{E}_{x \in G} \Re \langle \rho(x), V^* \rho^\prime(x) V\rangle_\sigma \nonumber \end{eqnarray} Because $\rho$ is unitary and ${\rm Tr} \sigma = 1$, $\mathbb{E}_{x \in G} \| \rho(x) \|_\sigma^2 = 1$. For the second term, recall from Eq.~\eqref{eq:isometry-average} that the compression is the group average $V^* \rho^\prime(x) V = \mathbb{E}_{y \in G} \rho^*(y)\rho(yx)$. Each summand $\rho^*(y)\rho(yx)$ is a product of unitaries, hence unitary, so $\|\rho^*(y)\rho(yx)\|_\sigma = 1$. By convexity of the $\sigma$-norm---the triangle inequality applied to the average---we obtain \begin{equation} \|V^* \rho^\prime(x) V\|_\sigma = \left\| \mathbb{E}_{y \in G} \rho^*(y)\rho(yx) \right\|_\sigma \le \mathbb{E}_{y \in G} \|\rho^*(y)\rho(yx)\|_\sigma = 1, \end{equation} hence $\mathbb{E}_{x \in G}\|V^* \rho^\prime(x) V\|_\sigma^2 \le 1$. Therefore using the bounds in ~Eq.~\eqref{eq:isometry-unitary-bound} and ~Eq.~\eqref{eq:inner-product-bound} by applying Lemma~\ref{gowers-hatami-correlation}, we have \begin{equation} \mathbb{E}_{x \in G}\left\|\rho(x)-V^{*} \rho^\prime(x) V\right\|_{\sigma}^{2} \le 2 - 2(1 - \varepsilon) = 2\varepsilon. \end{equation}

nodes.name: $G$ is an abelian group
nodes.statement: The operation $\star$ in~Eq.~\eqref{eq:star} makes $G$ into an abelian group with identity $e = (0, 1)$ and inverses $(x, a)^{-1} = (-a^2 x, a^{-1})$.
nodes.section: 2.4 BLR linearity test over $\FF_q$ via Gowers-Hatami
nodes.label: lem:group

nodes.statement: \emph{Associativity.} For $(x, a), (y, b), (z, c) \in G$, \begin{align*} \bigl((x, a) \star (y, b)\bigr) \star (z, c) &= (b^{-1}x + a^{-1}y,\; ab) \star (z, c) = \bigl(b^{-1}c^{-1}x + a^{-1}c^{-1}y + a^{-1}b^{-1}z,\; abc\bigr), \end{align*} and an identical computation gives the same expression for $(x, a) \star \bigl((y, b) \star (z, c)\bigr)$. \emph{Commutativity.} $(y, b) \star (x, a) = (a^{-1}y + b^{-1}x,\; ba) = (b^{-1}x + a^{-1}y,\; ab) = (x, a) \star (y, b).$ \emph{Identity.} For any $(y, b) \in G$, $(0, 1) \star (y, b) = (b^{-1}\cdot 0 + 1^{-1}\cdot y,\; 1\cdot b) = (y, b)$. \emph{Inverse.} For any $(x, a) \in G$, \[ (x, a) \star (-a^2 x, a^{-1}) = \bigl((a^{-1})^{-1}\cdot x + a^{-1}\cdot(-a^2 x),\; a\cdot a^{-1}\bigr) = (ax - ax,\; 1) = (0, 1). \]
nodes.section: 2.4 BLR linearity test over $\FF_q$ via Gowers-Hatami

nodes.name: Group isomorphism to product group
nodes.statement: The map \begin{equation} \Psi : G \to (X, +) \times (A, \cdot), \qquad \Psi(x, a) := (ax, a), \end{equation} is a group isomorphism onto the direct product of $(X, +)$ and $(A, \cdot)$ with operation $\star_\Psi:(x,\; a) \star_\Psi (y,\; b) = (x+y,\; ab)$. Indeed, \[ \Psi\bigl((x, a) \star (y, b)\bigr) = \bigl(ab\cdot(b^{-1}x + a^{-1}y),\; ab\bigr) = (ax + by,\; ab) = \Psi(x, a) \star_\Psi \Psi(y, b), \] and $\Psi$ is bijective with inverse $\Psi^{-1}(y, b) = (b^{-1}y, b)$. This isomorphism is used only to \emph{motivate} the characters below. The Lean development does not formalize $\Psi$: it equips $G$ with its group structure (Lemma~\ref{lem:group}) and defines the characters $\chi_{\alpha,k}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:group_characaters}) directly on the twisted group, proving the homomorphism property by direct computation rather than by pulling back through $\Psi$. Accordingly it is recorded as a remark, with no \texttt{\textbackslash lean} link and no node in the dependency graph.
nodes.section: 2.4 BLR linearity test over $\FF_q$ via Gowers-Hatami

nodes.name: Pontryagin dual over direct product
nodes.statement: For finite abelian groups $G_1, G_2$ with direct product $H = G_1 \times G_2$, the Pontryagin dual (the set of irreducible characters) factors as $\hat{H} = \hat{G_1} \times \hat{G_2}$. Like the isomorphism above, this is used only to motivate the character formula and is not part of the formalized graph.
nodes.section: 2.4 BLR linearity test over $\FF_q$ via Gowers-Hatami

nodes.name: Group characters
nodes.statement: The group $(G, \star)$ has the Pontryagin dual character group \begin{equation} \hat{G} = \{\chi_{\alpha, k}\}_{\alpha \in X, k \in [0, \cdots, q-2]}, \quad \chi_{\alpha, k}(x,a) = \omega^{{\rm Tr} \langle \alpha, a x \rangle} \psi_k(a), \end{equation} where $\psi_k(a) = e^{\frac{i 2 \pi m k}{q-1}}$ and $a=g_0^m$ for a fixed multiplicative generator $g_0\in A$.
nodes.section: 2.4 BLR linearity test over $\FF_q$ via Gowers-Hatami
nodes.label: prop:group_characaters

nodes.statement: By the isomorphism $\Psi(x, a) = (ax, a)$ in the remark above, $(G, \star) \cong (X, +) \times (A, \cdot)$. First we consider the characters of the product group. Using the Pontryagin-dual factorization in the remark above, we have \[ \widehat{(X, +) \times (A, \cdot)} = \hat{X} \times \hat{A}. \] The character groups of $X$ and $A$ are \begin{align} \hat{X} &= \{\phi_\alpha(y) = \omega^{{\rm Tr} \langle \alpha, y \rangle}\}_{\alpha\in X}, \\ \hat{A} &= \{\psi_k(b) =e^{\frac{i 2 \pi m k}{q-1}}\}_{k \in [0, \cdots, q-2]}, \end{align} where $b=g_0^m$ for a fixed multiplicative generator $g_0\in A$. Here the field trace ${\rm Tr}: \mathbb{F}_q \to \mathbb{F}_p$ is defined by ${\rm Tr}(x) = x + x^p + x^{p^2} + \cdots + x^{p^{s-1}}$ for $x \in \mathbb{F}_q$ (see Definition~1.1 in Chapter 1). Therefore, $\widehat{(X, +) \times (A, \cdot)} = \{\Theta_{\alpha, k}(y, b) = \phi_\alpha(y) \psi_k(b)\}_{\alpha, k}$. The character $\chi \in \hat{G}$ is given by the pull-back through the isomorphism \begin{equation} \chi_{\alpha, k}(x, a) = \Theta_{\alpha, k}(\Psi(x, a)) = \Theta_{\alpha, k}(ax, a). \end{equation} Therefore, we have $\chi_{\alpha, k}(x, a) = \phi_\alpha(ax) \psi_k(a) =\omega^{{\rm Tr} \langle \alpha, a x \rangle} \psi_k(a)$.

nodes.name: Matrix lift $F_f$
nodes.statement: Define a unitary matrix valued lift $F_f : G \to U(\mathbb{C}^{q-1})$ by the diagonal matrix \begin{equation} F_f(x, a) = D(a f(x)) := \sum_{c \in A} \omega^{{\rm Tr}\, c a f(x)}\mbox{$ | c \rangle $}\mbox{$ \langle c | $}, \end{equation} where $\{\mbox{$ | c \rangle $}\}$ denotes the orthonormal basis vectors of a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H} \cong \mathbb{C}^{q-1}$ and the inner product between operators defined by $\langle A, B \rangle_\sigma={\rm Tr}(A^* B \sigma)$ and choose $\sigma = \mathbb{I}/(q-1)$.

nodes.name: Soundness of the BLR test
nodes.statement: Let $q=p^s$ be a prime power. For every $f : \mathbb{F}_q^n \to \mathbb{F}_q$, $\delta(f, \ensuremath{\mathcal{LIN}}) \le \Pr_{a,b,x,y}\!\bigl[af(x) + bf(y) \ne f(ax + by)\bigr]$.
nodes.section: 2.4 BLR linearity test over $\FF_q$ via Gowers-Hatami
nodes.label: BLR_via_GH

nodes.statement: First denote \[ X := \mathbb{F}_q^n, \qquad A := \mathbb{F}_q^\times, \qquad \omega := e^{2\pi i/p}. \] Define a group $G$ on the set $X \times A$ with the binary operation \[ (x, a) \star (y, b) := \bigl(b^{-1}x + a^{-1}y,\; ab\bigr). \] Let $F_f$ be the unitary matrix valued lift $F_f : G \to U(\mathbb{C}^{q-1})$ given by the diagonal matrix \[ F_f(x, a) = D(a f(x)) := \sum_{c \in A} \omega^{{\rm Tr}\, c a f(x)}\mbox{$ | c \rangle $}\mbox{$ \langle c | $}, \] where $\{\mbox{$ | c \rangle $}\}$ denotes the orthonormal basis vectors of a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H} \cong \mathbb{C}^{q-1}$, the inner product between operators is $\langle A, B \rangle_\sigma={\rm Tr}(A^* B \sigma)$, and $\sigma = \mathbb{I}/(q-1)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:rep-iff-blr}, since $f$ is rejected with probability $\varepsilon$, the lift $F_f$ is a $(\frac{q}{q-1}\varepsilon,\frac{\mathbb{I}}{q-1})$ approximate representation of $(G, \star)$. Then by Lemma~\ref{lem:gh_linearity_formalized}, there exists a linear function $\ell: \mathbb{F}_q^n \to \mathbb{F}_q$ whose relative Hamming distance to $f$ is bounded by \[ \delta(f, \ell) \le \frac{q-1}{q}\cdot\frac{q}{q-1}\varepsilon = \varepsilon. \] This proves the claim \[ \delta(f, \ensuremath{\mathcal{LIN}}) := \min_{\alpha} \delta(f, \ell_\alpha) \leq \delta(f, \ell) \leq \varepsilon. \] Miraculously, the loose factor $\frac{q}{q-1}$ in the approximate-representation parameter cancels the tighter factor $\frac{q-1}{q}$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:gh_linearity_formalized}. In Lean this route is formalized as \texttt{gh\_blr\_soundness\_acceptance}, which proves \texttt{acceptanceProbabilityBLR f $\le$ 1 - distanceToLinear f} (the statement of \texttt{blr\_soundness}), valid for $\frac{q}{q-1}\varepsilon\le1$; the unconditional statement is the direct proof above, since for $\frac{q}{q-1}\varepsilon>1$ the third-moment extraction's $\max\ge0$ step fails.

nodes.statement: Let \(m,n >0\) be integers, \(\mathbb{F}\) be a field, \(R = \mathbb{F}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\) be its polynomial ring and \(R_{d}\) denote the subspace of polynomials of degree \(\leq d\). \[ \mathrm{QESAT}(\mathbb{F},n) := \{ (p_1, \ldots, p_m) \in R^m_{2} \mid \exists a \in \mathbb{F}^n, \, \forall i \in [m], \, p_i(a_1, \ldots, a_n) = 0 \}. \]
nodes.label: QESAT

nodes.name: Oracle specification
nodes.statement: An \emph{oracle specification} defines the type of the queries and outputs that an oracle can handle.
nodes.label: OracleSpec

nodes.statement: For this section, the \emph{randomness oracle specification} will be of a monadic function that takes nothing and returns an element from a field \(\mathbb{F}\).
nodes.label: randOracleSpec

nodes.name: Query implementation
nodes.statement: A \emph{query implementation} is a monadic function whose behavior conforms to a given oracle specification.
nodes.label: QueryImpl

nodes.statement: The \emph{uniform sampling query implementation} for a field \(\mathbb{F}\) is a (mathematical) query implementation for the randomness oracle specification that samples uniformly from \(\mathbb{F}\).
nodes.label: uniformSample

nodes.name: Implementing verifiers
nodes.statement: If we want to actually run the verifiers, we can also use concrete implementations based on the IO monad and system randomness for pseudorandom sampling.

nodes.name: Oracle context
nodes.statement: An \emph{oracle context} is a bundle consisting of an oracle specification and a query implementation for that specification.
nodes.label: OracleContext

nodes.name: Randomness oracle
nodes.statement: As \emph{randomness oracle}, we will use the {uniform sampling query implementation} for the randomness oracle specification.
nodes.label: randOracle

nodes.name: Oracle computation
nodes.statement: An \emph{oracle computation} is a monadic computation in the free monad generated by an oracle specification, i.e. a description (a ``script'') of a program consisting of a chain of oracle queries (compatible with any query implementation of the specification) and deterministic Lean computations.
nodes.label: OracleComp

nodes.name: Time complexity
nodes.statement: The price to pay for using these definitions for verifiers instead of Turing machines is that we have no simple way to enforce the time complexity of the verifier. For that, a possible approach would be to restrict the allowed operations to a strict set of operations instead of general Lean computations, and track the time cost using query complexity.
A \emph{PCP verifier} is a verifier with query access to a function $\pi : [\ell (|x|)] \to \Sigma$.
nodes.label: PCPVerifier

nodes.statement: A language $L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*$ is in $\mathrm{PCP}[\varepsilon_c, \varepsilon_s, \Sigma, \ell, q, r]$ if there exists a polynomial-time PCP verifier $V$ such that for every $x \in \{0,1\}^*$, $V$ makes at most $q(|x|)$ queries to the proof oracle and at most $r(|x|)$ randomness queries, and the following holds: \begin{itemize} \item Completeness: If $x \in L$, then $\exists \pi \in \Sigma^{\ell(|x|)}, \, \Pr\left[V^\pi(x)=1 \right] \geq 1 - \varepsilon_c$. \item Soundness: If $x \notin L$, then $\forall \widetilde{\pi} \in \Sigma^{\ell(|x|)},\, \Pr\left[V^{\widetilde{\pi}}(x)=1 \right] \leq \varepsilon_s$. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: PCP

nodes.statement: A \emph{LPCP verifier} is a verifier with query access to a linear function $\langle \pi,\cdot \rangle : \Sigma^{\ell(|x|)} \to \Sigma$.
nodes.label: LPCPVerifier

nodes.statement: A language $L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*$ is in $\mathrm{LPCP}[\varepsilon_c, \varepsilon_s, \Sigma, \ell, q, r]$ if there exists a polynomial-time LPCP verifier $V$ such that for every $x \in \{0,1\}^*$, $V$ makes at most $q(|x|)$ queries to the linear proof oracle and at most $r(|x|)$ randomness queries, and the following holds: \begin{itemize} \item Completeness: If $x \in L$, then $\exists \pi \in \Sigma^{\ell(|x|)}, \, \Pr\left[V^{\langle \pi, \cdot \rangle}(x)=1 \right] \geq 1 - \varepsilon_c$. \item Soundness: If $x \notin L$, then $\forall \widetilde{\pi} \in \Sigma^{\ell(|x|)},\, \Pr\left[V^{\langle \widetilde{\pi}, \cdot \rangle}(x)=1 \right] \leq \varepsilon_s$. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: LPCP

nodes.statement: Let \(V_{\mathrm{BLR}(\mathbb{F}_{2}, n)}^{f}\) be the verifier with oracle access to \(f: \mathbb{F}_{2}^n \to \mathbb{F}_{2}\) defined as follows: \begin{enumerate} \item Sample \(x, y \leftarrow \mathbb{F}_2^n\). \item Accept if and only if \(f(x) + f(y) = f(x+y)\). \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: BLR.basicVerifier

nodes.statement: Let \(n > 0\). For every linear function \(f: \mathbb{F}_{2}^n \to \mathbb{F}_{2}\), we have \[\Pr \left[V_{\mathrm{BLR}(\mathbb{F}_{2}, n)}^{f} = 1\right] = 1.\]
nodes.label: BLR_basic_completeness_ZMod2

nodes.statement: Let \(n > 0\) and \(f: \mathbb{F}_{2}^n \to \mathbb{F}_{2}\). \[\Pr \left[V_{\mathrm{BLR}(\mathbb{F}_{2}, n)}^{f} = 1\right] \leq 1 - \delta({f}, {\ensuremath{\mathcal{LIN}}}).\]
nodes.label: BLR_basic_soundness_ZMod2

nodes.statement: For a field \(\mathbb{F}\) and parameters \(m, n \in \mathbb{N}\), we define the language \[\mathrm{LINEQ}(\mathbb{F},m,n) := \{ (M, c) \in \mathbb{F}^{m\times n} \times \mathbb{F}^{m} \mid \exists b\in \mathbb{F}^n, \, Mb = c \}.\]
nodes.label: LINEQ

nodes.statement: Let \(V_{\mathrm{LINEQ}(\mathbb{F},m,n)}^{\langle b, \cdot \rangle } (M,c)\) be the LPCP verifier defined as follows: \begin{enumerate} \item Sample \(r \leftarrow \mathbb{F}^m\). \item Query \(b\in \mathbb{F}^n \) at \(u:= M^{\intercal}r \in \mathbb{F}^n\). \item Accept if and only if \(\langle b,u\rangle = \langle c, r\rangle\). \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: LINEQ.verifier

nodes.statement: Let \(a\in\mathbb{F}^m\) be nonzero. Then \[ |\mathbb{F}|\cdot\Pr_{r\leftarrow\mathbb{F}^m}\!\left[\langle a,r\rangle=0\right]\leq 1. \] Equivalently, a nonzero linear form over \(\mathbb{F}^m\) vanishes on a uniformly random input with probability at most \(1/|\mathbb{F}|\).
nodes.label: LINEQ.linear_form_uniform_prob_mul_card_le_one

nodes.statement: Choose a coordinate \(i\) with \(a_i\neq 0\). After fixing all other coordinates of \(r\), there is exactly one value of \(r_i\) making \(\langle a,r\rangle=0\).
\[\mathrm{LINEQ}(\mathbb{F},m,n) \in \mathrm{LPCP}\left[\varepsilon_c=0, \varepsilon_s= 1 / |\mathbb{F}|, \Sigma = \mathbb{F}, \ell = |x|, q = 1, r = m\right].\]
nodes.label: LINEQ_LPCP

nodes.statement: Consider the LPCP verifier \(V_{\mathrm{LINEQ}(\mathbb{F},m,n)}^{\langle b, \cdot \rangle } (M,c)\).\\ \emph{Completeness:} If \(Mb =c\), then for every \(r \in \mathbb{F}^m\), we have \[\langle b, u \rangle = b^{\intercal} (M^{\intercal} r) = (Mb)^{\intercal} r = \langle c , r\rangle.\] \emph{Soundness:} If \(Mb \neq c\), then \begin{gather*} \Pr_{r\leftarrow \mathbb{F}^m} \left[\langle b, u \rangle = \langle c , r\rangle \right] = \Pr_{r\leftarrow \mathbb{F}^m} \left[\langle Mb, r \rangle = \langle c , r\rangle \right] \\= \Pr_{r\leftarrow \mathbb{F}^m} \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{m} (Mb - c)_{i} \cdot r_{i} = 0\right] \leq 1 / |\mathbb{F}|, \end{gather*} where the last inequality follows from \ref{LINEQ.linear_form_uniform_prob_mul_card_le_one}.

For a field \(\mathbb{F}\) and \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), define the tensor test language \[ \mathrm{TENSORQ}(\mathbb{F}, n) := \bigl\{ (a, b) \in \mathbb{F}^n \times \mathbb{F}^{n^2} \mid b = \mathrm{flat}(a \otimes a) \bigr\}. \]
nodes.label: TENSORQ

nodes.statement: Given \((a,b) \in \mathbb{F}^n \times \mathbb{F}^{n^2}\), the LPCP verifier \(V_{\mathrm{TENSORQ}(\mathbb{F},n)}^{\langle \pi,\cdot\rangle}(a,b)\) uses a proof \(\pi=\alpha\parallel\beta \in \mathbb{F}^{n+n^2}\), intended to be the linear encoding of the public input \((a,b)\). Since the proof may be dishonest, the verifier checks consistency with \((a,b)\) on the sampled queries before checking the tensor relation: \begin{enumerate} \item Sample \(s,t \leftarrow \mathbb{F}^n\). \item Query the \(\alpha\)-part of \(\pi\) at \(s\) and at \(t\), obtaining \(y_s\) and \(y_t\). \item Query the \(\beta\)-part of \(\pi\) at \(\mathrm{flat}(s\otimes t)\), obtaining \(y_{s,t}\). \item Accept if and only if \[ y_s=\langle a,s\rangle,\qquad y_t=\langle a,t\rangle,\qquad y_{s,t}=\langle b,\mathrm{flat}(s\otimes t)\rangle,\qquad y_{s,t}=y_s y_t. \] \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: TENSORQ.verifier

nodes.statement: In settings where \(a\) and \(b\) are supplied only by the proof oracle, the tensor self-check uses the same three queries but has no public input to compare against. Given oracle access to \(\pi=\alpha\parallel\beta\in\mathbb{F}^{n+n^2}\), sample \(s,t\leftarrow\mathbb{F}^n\), query \[ y_s=\langle\alpha,s\rangle,\qquad y_t=\langle\alpha,t\rangle,\qquad y_{s,t}=\langle\beta,\mathrm{flat}(s\otimes t)\rangle, \] and accept if and only if \(y_{s,t}=y_s y_t\). This is the tensor component used inside the QESAT verifier.
nodes.label: TENSORQ.selfVerifier

nodes.statement: For every \(a,s,t\in\mathbb{F}^n\), \[ \langle \mathrm{flat}(a\otimes a),\mathrm{flat}(s\otimes t)\rangle = \langle a,s\rangle \langle a,t\rangle. \]

nodes.name: Chernoff bound
nodes.statement: Let $X_1,\dots, X_N$ be independent random variables over $\{0,1\}$, and let $\mu=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i = 1}^N X_i\right]$. For any $\Delta > 0$ one has \begin{equation*} \Pr\left[\sum_{i = 1}^N X_i \ge \mu+\Delta\right] \le \exp(-2\Delta^2/N) \end{equation*}
nodes.label: LPCPToPCP.chernoff_bound

nodes.statement: Write $p_i=\mathbb{E}[X_i]$, so that $\mu=\sum_{i=1}^N p_i$. We first prove the elementary exponential-moment estimate \[ \mathbb{E}[\exp(\lambda(X_i-p_i))]\le \exp(\lambda^2/8) \] for every $\lambda>0$ and every $i$. Since $X_i$ is $\{0,1\}$-valued, \[ \mathbb{E}[\exp(\lambda(X_i-p_i))] = (1-p_i)\exp(-\lambda p_i)+p_i\exp(\lambda(1-p_i)). \] Equivalently, it is enough to show \[ \log(1-p_i+p_i\exp(\lambda))-p_i\lambda \le \lambda^2/8. \] For $p\in[0,1]$, set $f(\lambda)=\log(1-p+p\exp(\lambda))-p\lambda$. Then $f(0)=f'(0)=0$, and \[ f''(\lambda) = \frac{p\exp(\lambda)}{1-p+p\exp(\lambda)} \left(1-\frac{p\exp(\lambda)}{1-p+p\exp(\lambda)}\right) \le \frac14. \] Hence, for $\lambda>0$, \[ f(\lambda) = \int_0^\lambda\int_0^u f''(v)\,dv\,du \le \int_0^\lambda\int_0^u \frac14\,dv\,du = \lambda^2/8. \] Let $S=\sum_{i=1}^N X_i$. By independence and the estimate above, \[ \mathbb{E}[\exp(\lambda(S-\mu))] = \prod_{i=1}^N \mathbb{E}[\exp(\lambda(X_i-p_i))] \le \exp(N\lambda^2/8). \] Markov's inequality gives, for every $\lambda>0$, \[ \Pr[S\ge \mu+\Delta] = \Pr[\exp(\lambda(S-\mu))\ge \exp(\lambda\Delta)] \le \exp(-\lambda\Delta)\mathbb{E}[\exp(\lambda(S-\mu))] \] Using the moment bound above, this is at most \[ \exp(-\lambda\Delta+N\lambda^2/8). \] Taking $\lambda=4\Delta/N$ gives \[ \Pr[S\ge \mu+\Delta]\le \exp(-2\Delta^2/N). \]

For an LPCP verifier making at most \(q\) linear queries, set \[ t := 8\bigl(\lfloor \log_2(100q)\rfloor+1\bigr). \] This is the concrete logarithmic shift count used in Lean. The converted PCP verifier uses \(t\) independent random shifts to decode each linear query by plurality.
nodes.label: LPCPToPCP.numShifts

nodes.name: Encoded proof
nodes.statement: For a linear LPCP proof \(\pi\in\mathbb{F}_2^\ell\), its PCP encoding \(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{lin}} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{\mathbb{F}_2^\ell}\) is the truth table \[ \widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{lin}}(a) := \langle \pi,a\rangle, \qquad a\in\mathbb{F}_2^\ell. \]
nodes.label: LPCPToPCP.encodedProof

nodes.statement: Given a PCP proof \(\widehat{\pi}:\mathbb{F}_2^\ell\to\mathbb{F}_2\), shifts \(r_1,\dots,r_t\in\mathbb{F}_2^\ell\), and a linear query \(a\in\mathbb{F}_2^\ell\), define the locally corrected answer \[ \mathsf{Corr}_{\widehat{\pi}}(a;r_1,\dots,r_t) := \operatorname{plurality}_{i\in[t]} \bigl(\widehat{\pi}(a+r_i)-\widehat{\pi}(r_i)\bigr). \]
nodes.label: LPCPToPCP.correctedAnswer

nodes.statement: Let \(V\) be an LPCP verifier over \(\mathbb{F}_2\). The converted PCP verifier \(\overline V\), with oracle access to \(\widehat{\pi}:\mathbb{F}_2^\ell\to\mathbb{F}_2\), proceeds as follows on input \(x\): \begin{enumerate} \item If \(V_{\mathrm{BLR}(\mathbb{F}_{2}, n)}^{\widehat{\pi}}=0\), reject. Otherwise, proceed to the next step. \item Sample \(t\) shifts \(r_1,\dots,r_t\in\mathbb{F}_2^\ell\), with \(t\) as in \ref{LPCPToPCP.numShifts}. \item Simulate \(V(x)\). Whenever \(V\) asks a linear query \(a\in\mathbb{F}_2^\ell\), answer it by \(\mathsf{Corr}_{\widehat{\pi}}(a;r_1,\dots,r_t)\). \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: LPCPToPCP.verifier

nodes.name: Completeness
nodes.statement: If \(\Pr\!\left[V^{\langle \pi, \cdot \rangle}(x)=1\right]\ge 1-\varepsilon_c\), then \(\Pr\!\left[\overline{V}^{\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{lin}}}(x)=1\right]\ge 1-\varepsilon_c\).
nodes.label: LPCPToPCP.verifier_completeness

nodes.statement: The encoded proof is linear, so the BLR test accepts with probability \(1\) by \ref{BLR_basic_completeness_ZMod2}. For every query \(a\) and every shift \(r_i\), \[ \widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{lin}}(a+r_i)-\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{lin}}(r_i) = \langle \pi,a\rangle. \] Thus every plurality answer equals the corresponding LPCP oracle answer, and the simulation has exactly the same acceptance probability as \(V\).

nodes.name: Soundness, far case
nodes.statement: If \(\delta({\widehat{\pi}}, {\ensuremath{\mathcal{LIN}}}) \geq 1 / 8\), then \[ \Pr[\overline V^{\widehat{\pi}}(x)=1]\leq 7/8 . \]
nodes.label: LPCPToPCP.verifier_soundness_far_case_of_isFar

nodes.statement: By \ref{BLR_basic_soundness_ZMod2}, the BLR precheck accepts with probability at most \(1-\delta({\widehat{\pi}}, {\ensuremath{\mathcal{LIN}}})\leq 7/8\). Since \(\overline V\) accepts only when this test accepts, its acceptance probability is at most \(7/8\).

If \(\delta({\widehat{\pi}}, {f}) < 1 / 8\) for some linear function \(f\) of the form \(u\mapsto\langle\pi,u\rangle\), then \[ \Pr_{r_1,\dots,r_t}\!\left[ \mathsf{Corr}_{\widehat{\pi}}(a;r_1,\dots,r_t)\neq \langle\pi,a\rangle \right] \leq \exp(-t/8), \quad \forall a\in\mathbb{F}_2^\ell. \]
nodes.label: LPCPToPCP.local_correction

nodes.statement: For one shift \(r\), the corrected sample can be wrong only if \(\widehat{\pi}(a+r)\) or \(\widehat{\pi}(r)\) disagrees \(f\). A union bound gives error probability at most \(2\cdot(1/8)=1/4\). If \(X_i\) is the indicator of failure for shift \(r_i\), then \(\mathbb{E}[\sum_i X_i]\le t/4\). The plurality answer is wrong only if \(\sum_i X_i\ge t/2\), so \ref{LPCPToPCP.chernoff_bound} with \(\Delta=t/4\) gives \(\exp(-t/8)\).

Assume every possible linear query \(a\) is locally corrected incorrectly with probability at most \(\eta\). If the simulated LPCP computation makes at most \(q\) proof queries, then its acceptance probability under the corrected PCP oracle is at most the acceptance probability under the nearby linear proof plus \(q\eta\).
nodes.label: LPCPToPCP.corrected_simulation_hybrid

nodes.statement: Expose the LPCP computation one oracle query at a time. At a proof query, the two simulations can diverge only when the local correction for the queried linear form is wrong; by assumption this has probability at most \(\eta\). Inducting over the query-bound derivation gives an additive loss of at most \(q\eta\).

nodes.name: Soundness, near case
nodes.statement: If \(x\notin L\), \(V\) has LPCP soundness \(\varepsilon_s\), and \(\delta({\widehat{\pi}}, {f}) < 1/8\) for some linear function \(f\) of the form \(u\mapsto\langle\pi,u\rangle\), then \[ \Pr[\overline V^{\widehat{\pi}}(x)=1]\leq \varepsilon_s+\frac{1}{100}. \]
nodes.label: LPCPToPCP.verifier_soundness_near_case

nodes.statement: By \ref{LPCPToPCP.local_correction}, every possible linear query has local correction error at most \(\eta=\exp(-t/8)\). The hybrid estimate \ref{LPCPToPCP.corrected_simulation_hybrid} compares the corrected simulation with the simulation using the nearby linear proof and loses at most \(q\eta\). The choice of \(t\) in \ref{LPCPToPCP.numShifts} gives \(q\eta\le 1/100\). The nearby linear proof is a valid LPCP proof, so its acceptance probability is at most \(\varepsilon_s\) because \(x\notin L\).

nodes.name: Soundness
nodes.statement: For every \(x\notin L\) and every PCP proof \(\widehat{\pi}\), \[ \Pr[\overline V^{\widehat{\pi}}(x)=1] \leq \max\{7/8,\varepsilon_s+1/100\}. \]
nodes.label: LPCPToPCP.verifier_soundness_of_cases

nodes.statement: If \(\delta({\widehat{\pi}}, {\ensuremath{\mathcal{LIN}}}) \geq 1 / 8\), apply \ref{LPCPToPCP.verifier_soundness_far_case_of_isFar}. Otherwise, apply \ref{LPCPToPCP.verifier_soundness_near_case}.

nodes.name: LPCPs admit exponential-size PCPs
nodes.statement: \begin{gather*} \mathrm{LPCP}[\varepsilon_c,\varepsilon_s,\Sigma=\mathbb{F}_{2},\ell,q,r] \subseteq\\ \mathrm{PCP}\left[ \varepsilon_c,\ \varepsilon_s'=\max\{7/8,\varepsilon_s+1/100\}, \Sigma'=\mathbb{F}_{2},\ \ell'=2^{\ell},\ q'=3+2tq,\ r'=r+(2+t)\ell \right]. \end{gather*}
nodes.label: LPCP_to_PCP_ZMod2

nodes.statement: Let $L \in \mathrm{LPCP}[\varepsilon_c,\varepsilon_s,\Sigma=\mathbb{F}_{2},\ell,q,r]$ and let $V$ be the LPCP verifier for $L$. Use the converted PCP verifier $\overline V$ defined in \ref{LPCPToPCP.verifier}. Completeness is \ref{LPCPToPCP.verifier_completeness}, and soundness is \ref{LPCPToPCP.verifier_soundness_of_cases}. The BLR test makes three proof queries. Each simulated LPCP query uses two PCP queries for each of the \(t\) shifts, so the query bound is \(3+2tq\). The randomness consists of the original \(r\) random bits, \(2\ell\) bits for the BLR test, and \(t\ell\) bits for the shifts.

Let \(x=(p_1,\dots,p_m) \in R_{2}^{m}\) be a QESAT instance as defined in \ref{QESAT}. Let \(V_{\mathrm{QESAT}(\mathbb{F}_2,n)}^{\pi}(x)\) be the LPCP verifier with oracle access to \(\pi=a\parallel b\in\mathbb{F}_2^{n+n^2}\), defined as follows: \begin{enumerate} \item Sample $r \gets \mathbb{F}_{2}^m$ and $s, t \gets \mathbb{F}_{2}^n$. \item Construct \((M_{x},c_{x}) \in \mathbb{F}_2^{m \times (n+n^2)} \times \mathbb{F}_2^m\) by the linearization above. \item Check that \(V_{\mathrm{LINEQ}(\mathbb{F}_2,m,n+n^2)}^{\langle \pi, \cdot \rangle } (M_{x},c_{x}) = 1\). \item Query \(\pi\) at \((s,0)\), \((t,0)\), and \((0,\mathrm{flat}(s\otimes t))\) and check that \[ \langle b,\mathrm{flat}(s\otimes t)\rangle =\langle a,s\rangle\langle a,t\rangle . \] Equivalently, this last step is the tensor self-check of \ref{TENSORQ.selfVerifier} specialized to \(\mathbb{F}_2\). \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: QESAT.verifier

nodes.name: Completeness
nodes.statement: If \(x\in \mathrm{QESAT}(\mathbb{F}_2,n)\), then exists a proof \(\pi\in\mathbb{F}_2^{n+n^2}\) such that \[\Pr\!\left[V_{\mathrm{QESAT}(\mathbb{F}_2,n)}^{\pi}(x)=1\right]=1.\]
nodes.label: QESAT.verifier_completeness

nodes.statement: Let \(a\in\mathbb{F}_2^n\) satisfy all equations and set \(b=\mathrm{flat}(a\otimes a)\). By construction of the linearized system, \(M_x(a\parallel b)=c_x\), so the LINEQ check accepts for every \(r\). The tensor self-check accepts for every \(s,t\) by \ref{TENSORQ.tensor_check_complete}.

nodes.name: Soundness
nodes.statement: If \(x\notin \mathrm{QESAT}(\mathbb{F}_2,n)\), then for every proof \(\tilde\pi\in\mathbb{F}_2^{n+n^2}\), \[\Pr\!\left[V_{\mathrm{QESAT}(\mathbb{F}_2,n)}^{\tilde\pi}(x)=1\right]\leq 3 / 4.\]
nodes.label: QESAT.verifier_soundness

nodes.statement:
If some \(p_i\) has total degree \(>2\), the verifier rejects immediately, so the acceptance probability is \(0\). Assume now that every \(p_i\) is quadratic and write \(\pi=a\parallel b\). If \(b
eq\mathrm{flat}(a\otimes a)\), then the tensor self-check accepts with probability at most \(3/4\) by ef{TENSORQ.selfVerifier_soundness_after_sampling} specialized to \(\mathbb{F}_2\), and the full verifier accepts only if that check accepts. Otherwise \(b=\mathrm{flat}(a\otimes a)\). Since \(x
otin\mathrm{QESAT}(\mathbb{F}_2,n)\), the assignment \(a\) does not satisfy all equations. By construction of the linearized system, \(M_x(a\parallel b)
eq c_x\). The LINEQ check therefore accepts with probability at most \(1/|\mathbb{F}_2|=1/2\) by ef{LINEQ.linear_form_uniform_prob_mul_card_le_one}. Again the full verifier accepts only if this check accepts, so the acceptance probability is at most \(1/2\leq 3/4\).
\[ \mathrm{QESAT}(\mathbb{F}_2,n) \in \mathrm{LPCP}[ \varepsilon_c = 0, \varepsilon_s = 3/4, \Sigma = \mathbb{F}_2, \ell = n + n^2, q = 4, r = |x| + 2n ]. \]
nodes.label: QESAT_poly_LPCP

nodes.statement: Use the verifier \ref{QESAT.verifier}. It makes one query for the LINEQ check and three queries for the tensor self-check, for a total of four. Its randomness is the LINEQ randomness plus two vectors in \(\mathbb{F}_2^n\). Completeness and soundness are \ref{QESAT.verifier_completeness} and \ref{QESAT.verifier_soundness}.
\[ \mathrm{QESAT}(\mathbb{F}_2,n) \in \mathrm{PCP}[ \varepsilon_c = 0, \varepsilon_s = 7/8, \Sigma = \mathbb{F}_2, \ell = 2^{|x|}, q = O(1), r = |x|^{O(1)} ]. \]
nodes.label: QESAT_exp_PCP_before_repetition

nodes.statement: Apply \ref{LPCP_to_PCP_ZMod2} to \ref{QESAT_poly_LPCP}. Since the LPCP soundness is \(3/4\), the converted soundness is \[ \max\{7/8,\,3/4+1/100\}=7/8. \] The query bound remains constant because \(q=4\), and the randomness is polynomial in the input size. The Lean formalization pads the proof oracle from length \(2^{n+n^2}\) to length \(2^{|x|}\).

Invoke \ref{QESAT_exp_PCP_before_repetition} to obtain the \(7/8\)-sound verifier. Run it independently six times and accept only if all six runs accept. Completeness error remains \(0\). For \(x\notin L\), the acceptance probability is at most \((7/8)^6\leq 1/2\). Query and randomness bounds are multiplied by the constant \(6\).
\[ \mathrm{QESAT}(\mathbb{F}_2,n) \in \mathrm{PCP}[ \varepsilon_c = 0, \varepsilon_s = 1/2, \Sigma = \mathbb{F}_2, \ell = 2^{|x|}, q = O(1), r = |x|^{O(1)} ]. \]
nodes.label: QESAT_exp_PCP

nodes.statement: Combine \ref{QESAT_exp_PCP_before_repetition} with the constant repetition step \ref{QESAT.constant_repetition}.
